name: radare2
one_line: reverse-engineering framework: disassembler, debugger and hex editor
plain: `radare2` (command `r2`) opens a program and lets you look at its machine code, step through it with a debugger, patch bytes and search for strings, all from one text prompt. It is a command-line alternative to Ghidra for fast triage.
It uses very short commands: `aaa` analyses, `afl` lists functions, `pdf` prints a function's disassembly. A question mark after any command shows its help (`a?`, `p?`, `?`).
Related tools in the same package: `rabin2` (file information and strings), `rasm2` (assemble and disassemble), `rax2` (convert numbers), `rahash2` (hashes), `radiff2` (compare binaries).
when: Quick look at what a binary does without opening a GUI.
Find the function that checks a password.
Run a program under a debugger and watch the registers.
Patch a jump so a check always passes.

examples.title: Open and analyse
examples.explain: -A runs the analysis (aaa) at start. You land at a prompt like [0x00401050]>.

examples.title: List functions
examples.explain: Prints every function found with its address and size. Look for main and for names such as check, verify, auth.

examples.title: Disassemble main
examples.explain: `s main` seeks to main, `pdf` prints the disassembly of the function. Read it for compares (cmp) and jumps (je, jne).

examples.title: Find strings
examples.explain: iz lists strings in the data section, izz searches the whole file. Strings like 'Correct!' lead you to the check.

examples.title: Cross-references
examples.explain: axt shows where a string or address is used: jump straight to the code that prints success.

examples.title: Visual mode
examples.explain: A full-screen view of the code. Press p to change the view, ? for help, q to leave.

examples.title: Debug it
examples.cmd:
r2 -d ./crackme
db main
dc
dr
dso
examples.explain: -d starts a debug session. db sets a breakpoint, dc continues, dr shows registers, dso steps over one instruction.

examples.title: Patch a jump
examples.explain: -w opens the file writable. wx writes hex bytes (9090 is two NOPs): the check can no longer fail. Work on a copy.

examples.title: File information
examples.explain: -I prints format, architecture and protections (PIE, NX, canary); -z lists strings.

examples.title: Assemble and disassemble
examples.explain: Turns assembly into bytes and the reverse, handy for patches and shellcode.

examples.title: Number conversion
examples.explain: Convert between hex and decimal, and from hex to a string.

options.plain: Quiet: no banner; with -c run a command and exit.
Run commands (separated by ;) then continue or quit with -q.
Seek to an address or name.
Strings / all strings / info / imports / sections.

Help for the command so far (append to any command).

mistakes: Patching the only copy of the binary: always copy first.
Forgetting to run aaa/-A, so afl is empty.
Using debug mode (-d) on untrusted malware outside a VM.
Reading AT&T-style syntax when you wanted Intel: set asm.syntax=intel.
try: Open a small crackme with r2 -A, find main, and read its compares.
Use iz and axt to find the success message and the code behind it.
Patch a jne to je and run the program.
Re-do the same job in Ghidra and compare the speed.
see_also: ghidra(1), gdb(1), objdump(1), readelf(1), checksec(1), strings(1), pwntools(7), Cutter (GUI for radare2).
